A.reason: All five are usable and have distinct primary mechanisms: recurring supply commitments, timed releases, voluntary category shares, staggered donation arrivals, and weekly demand-responsive requests. Candidate 0 best supports predictable replenishment with modest coordination, consistent allocation guidance and honest availability notices. The buffer is usable but may deny immediate requests; the other routes depend on donor flexibility, cooperation or sufficiently complete records.

B.reason: All candidates are usable. Candidate 5 repairs recurring commitments rather than introducing a new primary mechanism; candidate 6 similarly adjusts flexible shares. Low-stock-triggered requests and loss prevention are distinct mechanisms. Candidate 5 is best because it adds clear ownership, correction of missed-delivery expectations, duplicate-request prevention and a bounded fallback workload while preserving equal access and all required tracking.

pair.reason: B5 improves on A0 by specifying what happens when a commitment fails, a directly relevant threat to recipient predictability. Its fallback operates through existing visits, limits coordination costs and has an inspectable case review and stopping rule. These practical improvements justify the preference despite added complexity; effects remain unproven.
